v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e01 and writer brief a10e01-v1.0.0.md. a9e07's next field was honoured: a foundry's night shift, how a GPU works for people who don't write its code, computing versus moving data in and out of memory, and why writing an answer one word at a time waits on memory. Keeps apart from a8e07 (no break-even sums: here a card's speed, not an idle card's bill) and a10e10 (one card's speed per answer, not a fleet's cost); no bells, no conveyor line; the story is the rented card, not the casting. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 8.03 billion weights, 16.06 billion bytes in 16-bit, about 15 GB on the card's meter; the foundry's own writing curve on one A100 80GB, 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in a step (1 answer 10.25 ms, about 100 a second; 8 answers 12 ms); A100 80GB 2,039 GB/s and 312 TFLOPS dense; L40S 864 GB/s and 362 TFLOPS dense (733 with sparsity). The foundry's own measurements, never a source's: writing reaches about 80% of the road's limit (100 and 43 a second), reading runs at about half the sheet's sums a second. Timeline: launch Monday 6 July 2026 on the A100 at $2.79 an hour; the IT contractor compared the two sheets on TFLOPS the week before; the works manager signed on Tuesday 29 September; the rental moved to the L40S at $1.54 an hour at 00:00 on Thursday 1 October ($1,124 against $2,037 for a 730-hour month); at 00:40 two short answers of about 30 tokens took 0.88 s each (0.51 s on the A100), so nothing looked wrong; at 01:20, ladle 3 due at 01:30, the 600-token checklist took 14.1 s (6.2 s on Thursday 24 September), which is what alerted the melter; ladle 3 poured at 01:31 from the paper process sheet; the post at about 01:40. Cold case: 4 months later, Friday 2 October 2026 to Monday 11 January 2027. Prices are the story's given data: Lambda's list showed $2.79 for the A100 80GB SXM when read on 16 October 2026; the L40S's $1.54 is the story's own figure, close to the median of $1.50 that the aggregator GetDeploying showed when read on 16 October 2026 (33 providers with a priced on-demand config, last updated 16 October 2026; the bible's reading of 15 October said $1.54 across 32). Contracts are stated conditionally; not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: The Furnace

post.author: u/ladle_three_tirzah
post.title: I'm the night melter at an iron foundry. At midnight our assistant moved to a card whose sheet says it's faster. At 01:20 the pouring checklist dripped out for 14 seconds.

blocks.text: I'm Tirzah, night melter at Corriveau Castings, an iron foundry. We melt iron in an electric furnace and pour it from a ladle, a lined bucket on a crane, into sand moulds for pump housings. On Thursday 1 October, ladle 3 was due at 01:30.

Since Monday 6 July our assistant has answered questions from 3,000 pages of process sheets, the foundry's written rules for each job, and written the ladle checklists. It's a language model: a program that writes text in small pieces, often part of a word, called tokens.
Ours is Meta's Llama 3.1 8B: a file of 8.03 billion learned numbers, called its weights.
Each weight is stored in 16 bits, the space of two bytes, so the file holds 16.06 billion bytes.

It runs on a rented graphics card: a chip of thousands of small adders, fed numbers by one fast memory road. Venkatesh, our IT contractor, calls it a fast cook fed through one narrow hatch. The proper name is a GPU, a graphics processing unit.

Customers send us drawings. If a customer's contract says its drawings stay on systems the foundry controls, a shared pay-per-token service is out; that's how our works manager reads ours, and this isn't legal advice. So we rent a whole card by the hour.

Every card has a sheet: the maker's list of its numbers. One is sums a second, given in TFLOPS, short for trillion floating-point operations per second: sums on numbers with a decimal point, each one multiplication or addition.
Another is memory speed: how many GB, billions of bytes, the road carries each second. Our weights fill about 15 GB on the card's own meter.

An answer takes two steps. First the card reads the question, about 2,000 tokens with the pages it pulls in, all in one pass. Then it writes, one token at a time: it reads every weight once, adds one token, and repeats.

Since launch it has run on an NVIDIA A100 80GB at $2.79 an hour. Last week Venkatesh compared its sheet with an NVIDIA L40S's: 362 TFLOPS against 312, for $1.54 an hour, $1,124 a 730-hour month instead of $2,037. The works manager signed on Tuesday; the rental moved at 00:00 Thursday.
At 00:40 I asked which mould line and which sand mix. Both answers, about 30 tokens each, came in under a second, as always.
At 01:20 I asked for ladle 3's pouring checklist, about 600 tokens. The first word appeared at once.
Then the rest dripped out, word by word, like iron from a choked spout.
Fourteen seconds, with the crane waiting; last Thursday it took 6. On the assistant's dashboard, each line shows the day, the card, the first token's wait, the speed after it, and the whole answer.

24 Sep 01:20  A100  first token 0.21 s  then 100 a second  600 tokens   6.2 s
01 Oct 01:20  L40S  first token 0.18 s  then 43 a second   600 tokens  14.1 s
The first token came sooner than ever. Every token after it came 2.3 times slower, on a card whose sheet says it's faster.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that furnace office is haunted, though the drip sounds grim. Your card has two limits, like your cook: how fast the adders can do sums, and how fast the road brings them numbers. Whichever runs out first sets the pace, and the other waits. Your dashboard timed two different jobs: reading the question, and writing the answer. Two questions. For each card, how many bytes does writing one token have to fetch, and how fast does that card's road carry them? And how many sums does it do with each byte once it arrives?

replies.author: u/ladle_three_tirzah
replies.text: Writing one token fetches all 16.06 billion bytes of weights. The A100's sheet says its road carries 2,039 GB/s; the L40S's says 864. The sums I haven't counted yet.

comments.author: u/sheet_never_lies_venkatesh
comments.text: 362 beats 312. The sheet doesn't lie: the L40S does more sums a second, and the first token proves it, 0.18 s against 0.21. Something else broke tonight, a setting or the network. And if the card really is short, rent one whose sheet shows even more. The L40S's own sheet prints 733.

replies.author: u/ladle_three_tirzah
replies.text: Next to the 733 is an asterisk: With Sparsity. You told me that's a mode that skips sums on weights thinned out to zero in a special pattern. Ours aren't thinned.

replies.author: u/sheet_never_lies_venkatesh
replies.text: Then a card that does more without it. More sums is more sums.

comments.author: u/day_shift_caoimhe
comments.text: Day-shift process engineer here. Every question drags about 2,000 tokens of process sheets in with it. Trim the pages it pulls in to the best 1,000 tokens' worth and the card has half as much to read before it writes a word. Shorter questions, quicker answers.

replies.author: u/ladle_three_tirzah
replies.text: Tonight the first token came in 0.18 s.

comments.author: u/one_byte_chinonso
comments.text: Whatever the card fetches, fetch less of it. Store the weights in 8 bits, one byte each instead of two, and the file is half the size. Plenty of people serve models that way.

replies.author: u/ladle_three_tirzah
replies.text: The checklists carry pour temperatures and alloy weights. Has anyone checked that an 8-bit copy writes the same ones?

reply.prompt: It's 01:40 on Thursday 1 October, and the works manager is in at 07:00. What should the foundry change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Rent a card whose sheet shows even more sums a second than the L40S.
options.part2: At 07:00 the works manager agreed to try Venkatesh's way, and by Friday he had shortlisted a card whose sheet showed more sums a second than the L40S, on the same 864 GB/s road and at about the same price. Before renting it I replayed it in the sim at 733 trillion sums a second: reading the question fell from 0.18 s to 0.09 s. Writing stayed at about 43 a second, the checklist still took 14 s, and a million tokens still cost $9.95. The sums per byte told me why: writing does 1, and this card could do 848. The adders were never what we waited on.
options.senior: A sheet's headline counts the adders, and writing waits on the road. Each token fetches all 16.06 billion bytes, so 864 GB/s caps writing at about 54 a second however many sums a card can do. And the L40S's 733 is marked with sparsity, which only helps weights thinned in a special pattern. More sums speed up reading the question, which took 0.18 s of 14.

options.text: Shorten the questions so the card has fewer tokens to read per answer.
options.part2: On Thursday afternoon Caoimhe trimmed the pages the assistant pulls in, so each question came to about 1,000 tokens instead of 2,000. In the sim, reading the question fell from 0.18 s to 0.09 s. Writing stayed at 43 a second. On Friday night ladle 3's checklist still took 14 s, and the assistant now answered from half as many process-sheet pages. We saved a tenth of a second and lost half our references.
options.senior: Reading the question is one pass that uses each fetched weight for all 2,000 tokens, so it is limited by the adders and was already fast: 0.18 s. The 14 seconds were writing, 600 tokens one at a time, each fetching every weight. Shortening the input trims the small part and leaves the large part untouched, and costs the answer its sources.

options.text: Compare cards by memory speed per dollar, timed on our own answers.
options.part2: At 07:00 I showed the works manager the sum by hand. Each token fetches 16.06 billion bytes: on the A100's road, 16.06 ÷ 2,039 = 7.9 ms, at most 127 a second; on the L40S's, 18.6 ms, at most 54. Per dollar, the A100 carries 2,039 GB/s for $2.79 an hour, about 731 a dollar; the L40S 864 for $1.54, about 561. A million tokens cost $7.75 on the A100 ($2.79 ÷ 360,000 tokens an hour) and $9.95 on the L40S ($1.54 ÷ 154,800). The cheaper card was dearer per token. Venkatesh moved the rental back to the A100 at 00:00 on Friday 2 October, after replaying last week's questions from the dashboard on it: first token 0.21 s, about 100 a second, the checklist in 6 s. The works manager added a rule: no card changes until the new card is timed on our own answers, and compared by memory speed per dollar.
options.senior: For writing one answer at a time, the card's memory speed sets the pace: every token fetches every weight, and the adders do about one sum per byte while the A100 could do 153. So compare cards by GB/s per dollar and by cost per million tokens at the speed you measure, not by the headline sums a second. Then time the new card on your own questions before the switch, because the sheet measures the card, not your work.

options.text: Keep the cheaper card and store the weights in 8 bits to halve reads.
options.part2: Venkatesh made an 8-bit copy, FP8 (short for 8-bit floating point), one byte per weight, and switched to it on the L40S at 00:00 on Friday 2 October. In the sim: 8.03 billion bytes a token, 9.3 ms on the road, about 86 a second, the checklist in 7 s, a million tokens for $4.97, still $1,124 a month. Faster and cheaper. But nobody had scored the 8-bit copy against the 16-bit one on our own checklists, with their pour temperatures and alloy weights. Until someone does, the works manager ruled, every checklist is checked against the process sheet by hand before the ladle moves.
options.senior: Halving the bytes per token halves what the road carries for each token, so writing nearly doubles: 864 ÷ 8.03 × 0.8 = about 86 a second. It is the right lever, because it acts on the road. But a squeezed model is a different model, and the numbers it writes are what matter in a pouring checklist. It is a trade-off you take only after measuring the quality lost on your own tasks, which a later case in this season teaches.

sim.title: Time the assistant on each card
sim.lede: You're Tirzah at 23:50 on Wednesday 30 September, on the A100, before the rental moves. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 8B has 8.03 billion weights, 2 bytes each in 16 bits (16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB on the card's meter) and 1 byte each in 8 bits. The A100 80GB: 2,039 GB/s, 312 TFLOPS, $2.79 an hour. The L40S: 864 GB/s, 362 TFLOPS, $1.54 an hour. A card with more sums on the same road: 864 GB/s, 733 TFLOPS (the L40S sheet's figure with sparsity), priced like the L40S. Writing a token fetches every weight once, so the road's limit is bytes ÷ memory speed. Two of the foundry's own measurements: writing reaches about 80% of the road's limit (the dashboard's 100 and 43 a second; every other setting is an estimate at 80%, rounded to two figures), and reading the question runs at about half the sheet's sums a second, with 2 sums per weight for each token read (kept at the 16-bit rate in every setting). A question is 2,000 tokens with its pages; a checklist is 600. A month is 730 hours.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the A100 opens at 7.9 ms a token on the road, at most 127 a second, about 100; reading 0.21 s; the checklist 6 s; $7.75 per million. Play the night: the L40S at 00:00, 18.6 ms, at most 54, about 43, reading 0.18 s, the checklist 14 s, $9.95. Read the sums per byte: writing does 1, the A100 could do 153, the L40S 419. Pick the card with more sums on the same road: reading 0.09 s, writing still 43. Set the question to 1,000 tokens: reading halves, the checklist doesn't move. Switch to 8 bits on the L40S: about 86. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the foundry was haunted. Writing each token fetches all 16.06 billion bytes of weights once, so its speed is set by the card's memory road, not its adders: 2,039 GB/s on the A100 gave about 100 tokens a second, 864 GB/s on the L40S about 43. The L40S's bigger sum count only sped up reading the question, from 0.21 s to 0.18 s, and the cheaper card cost more per token: $9.95 a million against $7.75.

steps.title: Writing one token, step by step.
steps.text: First, the card fetches every weight from its memory, all 16.06 billion bytes, over the memory road. Second, its adders do about two sums per weight, one multiplication and one addition, to pick the next token. Third, it adds that token to the answer. Then it repeats, once per token. The road sets the floor: 16.06 ÷ 2,039 GB/s = 7.9 ms on the A100, at most 127 tokens a second; 16.06 ÷ 864 = 18.6 ms on the L40S, at most 54. The foundry's own writing curve on the A100 is 10 ms a step plus 0.25 ms per answer in it, 10.25 ms for one answer, about 100 a second: about 80% of the road. Tonight's dashboard showed 43 on the L40S, 80% of 54. What can go wrong: at the first step, a narrower road makes every token wait, whatever the adders could do.

steps.title: Reading the question is the opposite job.
steps.text: Reading happens in one pass. First, the card fetches each weight once. Then it uses it for all 2,000 tokens of the question before moving on: 2 × 8.03 billion × 2,000 = 32 trillion sums from one fetch of the weights. That job is limited by the adders. At about half the sheet's rate, the foundry's own measurement, it takes 32.12 ÷ 156 = 0.21 s on the A100 and 32.12 ÷ 181 = 0.18 s on the L40S. So the first token came sooner and every later token came slower. What can go wrong: a test that times only the first token sees the new card win.

steps.title: Sums per byte decides which limit you hit.
steps.text: NVIDIA's GPU Performance Background User's Guide calls the sums an algorithm does per byte it fetches its arithmetic intensity, and the card's sums a second divided by its bytes a second its ops:byte ratio. If the job's sums per byte are lower than the card's ratio, the job is memory limited; if higher, math limited. The A100's ratio is 312 ÷ 2.039 = 153; the L40S's 362 ÷ 0.864 = 419. Writing for one person does 1 sum per byte: memory limited on both, with the adders idle most of the time. Reading 2,000 tokens does 2,000: math limited on both. The headline TFLOPS counts the adders, and writing waits on the road. One fetch of the weights can serve every answer written in the same step, which is why serving many people at once is cheap: on the foundry's curve, 8 answers take 12 ms a step, not 8 × 10.25. Later cases in this season build on that. What can go wrong: a card's ratio rises when its adders grow faster than its road, so a newer card can be worse at writing.

steps.title: The cheaper card cost more per token.
steps.text: Cost per million tokens is the price per hour divided by the tokens an hour. The A100: 100 a second × 3,600 = 360,000 an hour; $2.79 ÷ 360,000 × 1,000,000 = $7.75. The L40S: 43 × 3,600 = 154,800; $1.54 ÷ 154,800 × 1,000,000 = $9.95. Per dollar the A100 also has the wider road: 2,039 ÷ 2.79 = 731 GB/s for each dollar an hour, against 864 ÷ 1.54 = 561. a8e07's card billed every hour, busy or idle; here every hour costs the same and writes 2.3 times fewer tokens. Dead Letter's s9e04 put cost per unit of business on the bill; here the unit is a million tokens. What can go wrong: a monthly saving of $913 hides a dearer token.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the one that half works.
steps.text: A card whose sheet shows more sums on the same road reads faster and writes no faster: the L40S's own 733 is marked with sparsity, which only helps weights thinned in a special pattern. Shorter questions trim the 0.18 s of reading and leave the 14 s of writing. Serving more people at once writes more tokens in total and none faster for the melter. Storing the weights in 8 bits, FP8, halves the bytes per token: 864 ÷ 8.03 × 0.8 = about 86 a second on the L40S. That works on the right limit, but a squeezed model is a different model, and its quality on our own checklists has to be measured first. What can go wrong: a squeeze tested only on easy text can still change a pour temperature.

diagram.aria: How one token is written on each card. Top row, the A100: the weights, 16.06 billion bytes, fetched once a token; the road, 2,039 GB/s, 7.9 ms a token; the adders, 312 trillion sums a second, able to do 153 sums per byte; the checklist at about 100 a second, 600 tokens in 6 s. Bottom row, the L40S: the same weights; the road, 864 GB/s, 18.6 ms a token; the adders, 362 trillion sums a second, able to do 419 sums per byte; the checklist at about 43 a second, 14 s. A note: writing uses 1 sum per byte, so the road sets the speed.

notes.text: The A100: a wide road, adders mostly idle
The L40S: more adders, a narrower road
Writing uses 1 sum per byte fetched, so the road sets the speed

explain.caption: Read each row left to right, once per token: the weights are fetched over the road, the adders do their sums, and one token joins the checklist. On both cards the adders could do far more sums per byte than writing needs, 153 and 419 against 1, so they wait, and the road's width sets the speed: 7.9 ms a token on the A100, 18.6 ms on the L40S.

fix.title: The fix: compare cards by memory speed per dollar, and time them on our own answers
fix.text: Move back to the A100 (or any card with an equal road): 2,039 GB/s for $2.79 an hour is about 731 GB/s a dollar, against the L40S's 561, and a million tokens cost $7.75 against $9.95. Before any card change, do the sum by hand: bytes per token ÷ memory speed gives the road's limit, and price per hour ÷ tokens an hour gives the cost per million. Then replay a set of our own questions and checklists on the new card and time both the first token and the speed after it. Only switch when both hold. Write the rule down, so the next sheet comparison starts from memory speed, not the headline sums a second.

limits: Memory speed per dollar predicts writing for one answer at a time. With many answers sharing each step, or very long questions, the sums can matter again, so time your own mix of work.

The 80% of the road and the half-rate reading are the foundry's own measurements on two cards. Another card, driver or serving program can land elsewhere, which is why the replay on your own answers matters.
Prices move. The A100's $2.79 is one provider's list price and the L40S's $1.54 sits close to an aggregator's median, so do the sum again when either changes.

explain.seniorTake: A GPU is two machines in one box: thousands of adders and one memory road, and every job is limited by whichever it runs out of first. Writing text for one person fetches every weight for every token and does about one sum per byte, far below any modern card's ops:byte ratio, so it waits on the road; reading a long question uses each fetched weight thousands of times and waits on the adders. A sheet's headline TFLOPS describes the adders, so a card chosen by it can read faster and write slower, as the L40S did here: 0.18 s to the first token, then 43 a second instead of 100. Compare cards for writing by memory speed per dollar and by cost per million tokens at the speed you measure, and time the new card on your own questions before the switch. Storing the weights in fewer bits acts on the right limit but changes the model, so it waits for a quality check. And the cheap way to more tokens is more answers in each step, because one fetch of the weights can serve them all.

realWorld.title: NVIDIA: arithmetic intensity and the ops:byte ratio
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's GPU Performance Background User's Guide divides operations by bytes accessed, which is known as the algorithm’s arithmetic intensity, and divides a processor's math rate by its memory bandwidth, which is sometimes called ops:byte ratio. It says an algorithm is math limited on a given processor if the algorithm’s arithmetic intensity is higher than the processor’s ratio, and memory limited when it is lower. The same page describes an A100 with up to 2039 GB/s bandwidth from 80 GB of HBM2 memory and gives 312 FP16 TFLOPS of dense math.

realWorld.title: NVIDIA: one vector at a time is memory limited
realWorld.text: The same guide takes a fully-connected layer applied to a single vector, a batch of one, and says it is memory limited. Writing one answer at a time is that case: each token multiplies the weights by one small list of numbers. The guide also says NVIDIA® GPUs consist of a number of Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the blocks that hold the adders.

realWorld.title: The A100 80GB's sheet
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's A100 page lists GPU memory bandwidth of 2,039 GB/s for the 80GB SXM card, and its FP16 Tensor Core row reads 312 TFLOPS | 624 TFLOPS*, with the footnote * With sparsity. The story uses the dense 312.

realWorld.title: The L40S's sheet
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's L40S page lists memory bandwidth of 864GB/s and 48GB GDDR6 with ECC. Its FP16 Tensor Core row gives 362.05, and 733 marked with an asterisk, footnoted *With Sparsity. The story uses the dense 362; the 733 is the figure the contractor's comment points at.

realWorld.title: Llama 3, Table 3: the 8B model's shape
realWorld.text: The Llama 3 paper's Table 3, Overview of the key hyperparameters of Llama 3, gives the 8B model 32 layers, a model dimension of 4,096, 32 attention heads and 8 key/value heads, 128 numbers each (4,096 ÷ 32). The story's 8.03 billion weights and 16.06 billion bytes are the shared given data for this season.

realWorld.title: CUDA Programming Guide: what a GPU is for
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's CUDA Programming Guide says GPUs are specialized for highly parallel computations and that a GPU is designed to excel at executing thousands of threads in parallel: many small workers at once, the thousands of adders in this story.

realWorld.title: The prices: one provider's list and an aggregator's median
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists NVIDIA A100 SXM, 80 GB, at $2.79 a GPU an hour: the story's A100 price is close to this list price. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

realWorld.title: GetDeploying's L40S page: an aggregator's median
realWorld.text: GetDeploying, an aggregator, said on 16 October 2026 that the median on-demand price is $1.50 per GPU per hour across 33 providers with a priced on-demand config, and Last updated Oct. 16, 2026. The story's $1.54 is its own given figure, close to that median. A median across many providers is not any one provider's offer.

asked: Why is generating text memory-bound on a GPU?
How would you choose between two GPUs for one small model?
interview.answer: Generating text writes one token at a time, and each token needs every weight fetched from the card's memory once. For an 8-billion-weight model in 16 bits that's about 16 GB per token, with about two sums per weight, so roughly one sum per byte fetched. An A100 can do about 153 sums for every byte its memory delivers (312 TFLOPS over 2,039 GB/s), so the adders mostly wait: the job's arithmetic intensity is far below the card's ops:byte ratio, which makes it memory-bound. Reading the prompt is the opposite: each fetched weight is used for every prompt token, so it is compute-bound. To choose between two cards for one small model, I'd first do the sum by hand: bytes per token divided by memory bandwidth gives the ceiling on tokens a second, and price per hour divided by tokens an hour gives cost per million. I once saw a card with a higher TFLOPS figure and less than half the bandwidth: the first token came sooner, every later token 2.3 times slower, and a million tokens cost more despite the lower hourly price. Then I'd time both cards on our own prompts, measuring time to the first token and tokens a second after it, and only then switch. If many users share the card, batching changes the picture, because one fetch of the weights serves every answer in the step, so I'd test at our real concurrency too.

terms.def: A works that melts metal and pours it into moulds to make castings. Corriveau Castings melts iron for pump housings.
The foundry worker who runs the furnace through the night and readies each ladle for pouring. Tirzah is Corriveau's.
A lined bucket, carried on a crane, that takes molten iron from the furnace to the moulds. Ladle 3 was due to pour at 01:30.
The outer iron casing of a pump. The foundry casts them in sand moulds.
The foundry's written rules for each job, 3,000 pages of them. The assistant answers from them.
The list of checks before a ladle pours, written by the assistant: about 600 tokens. It took 6 s on the A100 and 14 s on the L40S.
A program that writes text in small pieces, one after another, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). The question is about 2,000 tokens; a checklist about 600.
The learned numbers a model is made of, stored in one file (a1e02). Llama 3.1 8B has 8.03 billion of them.
Meta's open-weights language model with 8.03 billion weights, 32 layers and 8 key/value heads (a1e08, a8e07). In 16 bits its file is 16.06 billion bytes.
One of the model's stacked stages; every token passes through all of them in turn. Llama 3.1 8B has 32.
Parts of each layer that keep short notes on earlier tokens. Llama 3.1 8B has 8 per layer, 128 numbers each. A later case in this season uses them.
The text sent to a model to answer: here the melter's question with the process-sheet pages it pulls in, about 2,000 tokens (a2e01).
Several answers written together, sharing each step's fetch of the weights. On the foundry's curve, 8 answers take 12 ms a step instead of 10.25 ms for one.
A bit is one 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits. A weight stored in 16 bits takes two bytes; in 8 bits, one.
Gigabyte, about a billion bytes. The card's meter counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB, so 16.06 billion bytes shows as about 15 GB; memory speeds use the maker's 1,000.
Graphics processing unit, the chip on a graphics card: thousands of small adders fed numbers by one fast memory road, like a fast cook fed through one narrow hatch.
Short for graphics card, the GPU and its memory on one board. The foundry rents one whole, by the hour.
This case's word for the GPU's many small units that do sums, multiplications and additions, all at once.
This case's word for the link that carries numbers from a card's memory to its adders. Its speed is the card's memory speed.
How many bytes a card's memory can deliver each second, in GB/s; also called memory bandwidth. The A100's is 2,039 GB/s, the L40S's 864.
A maker's list of a card's numbers, such as its sums a second and memory speed. Its headline figure counts the adders.
Short for trillion floating-point operations per second: sums a second on numbers with a decimal point. The A100's sheet says 312 (16-bit, dense), the L40S's 362.
This case's plain name for TFLOPS: how many multiplications or additions a card's adders can do each second.
Counted for ordinary weights, without the sparsity trick. The story uses dense figures: 312 and 362.
A mode that skips sums on weights thinned to zero in a special pattern. The L40S sheet's 733 is with sparsity; the foundry's weights aren't thinned.
The card the assistant ran on from launch: 2,039 GB/s memory speed and 312 TFLOPS dense, rented at $2.79 an hour.
The card the rental moved to at 00:00 on 1 October: 864 GB/s and 362 TFLOPS dense, at $1.54 an hour, with 48 GB of memory.
The first step of an answer: the card fetches each weight once and uses it for all 2,000 tokens in one pass. It is limited by the adders.
The second step: one token at a time, fetching every weight for each token. Fetch, sum, add one token, repeat. It is limited by the memory road.
The first piece of an answer, which appears once the question is read: 0.21 s on the A100, 0.18 s on the L40S.
How fast an answer is written after the first token: about 100 on the A100, 43 on the L40S.
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second. On the A100's road one token takes at least 7.9 ms.
The most tokens a second the memory road allows: memory speed ÷ bytes per token. 127 on the A100, 54 on the L40S, in 16 bits.
The foundry's own timing of the A100: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in it. One answer, 10.25 ms; 8 answers, 12 ms.
One pass of writing in which every answer being written gets one more token. One fetch of the weights serves every answer in the step.
A job's sums per byte fetched from memory. Writing for one person: about 1. Reading a 2,000-token question: about 2,000.
This case's plain name for arithmetic intensity, and, for a card, its sums a second ÷ its bytes a second.
A card's sums a second divided by its memory's bytes a second: 312 ÷ 2.039 = 153 for the A100, 362 ÷ 0.864 = 419 for the L40S.
Waiting on the memory road, because the job's sums per byte are below the card's ratio. Writing one answer is memory limited (memory-bound).
Waiting on the adders, because the job's sums per byte are above the card's ratio. Reading a long question is math limited (compute-bound).
Price per hour ÷ tokens written an hour × 1,000,000. $2.79 ÷ 360,000 = $7.75 on the A100; $1.54 ÷ 154,800 = $9.95 on the L40S.
A card's GB/s divided by its price per hour: 731 for the A100 at $2.79, 561 for the L40S at $1.54.
Short for 8-bit floating point: each weight stored in one byte instead of two. It halves the bytes per token but changes the model, so its quality is measured first.
A provider's model that many customers use, charged per token (a8e07). If a contract keeps drawings on systems the foundry controls, it is ruled out. Not legal advice.
The assistant's screen of timings: for each answer, the card, the first token's wait, the tokens a second after it and the whole answer.
A website that collects many providers' prices in one place. GetDeploying is one; its median is not any one provider's price.
The middle value when prices are put in order: half the providers charge less, half more.
NVIDIA's name for one of the blocks a GPU is built from, each holding many adders. An A100 has 108.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A 8.32 covers change management; 5.23 covers the use of cloud services.
The course's hands-on builds. The Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this case's card choice when it compares a small self-hosted model with an API model.

atWork: Look for a GPU chosen from its sheet's headline TFLOPS. It is a common pattern: a cheaper card with a bigger sum count replaces the old one, the first token arrives sooner, every token after it arrives slower, and the cost per million tokens rises while the monthly bill falls. Ask four things. How many bytes does one token fetch (the model's size in bytes), and what is each card's memory speed? What is the road's limit on each, and the cost per million at the speed you measure? Has the new card been timed on your own prompts, both the first token and the speed after it? And how many answers share each step at your real traffic, since one fetch can serve them all? Build Night: the Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this card choice; a later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.32 (change management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for a test on real answers before a card change goes live, with the result recorded; and one checking 5.23 (information security for use of cloud services) would look for rental terms that cover where customers' drawings may go. If a customer's contract says its drawings stay on systems you control, check the rental's terms against it before any move. Neither note is legal advice.

recall.prompt: A clinic's notes assistant runs a model whose weights take 14 billion bytes, on a rented card that carries 1,000 GB/s, mostly for one doctor at a time. A seller offers a card with twice the TFLOPS and the same GB/s at the same price, promising answers twice as fast. What do you tell the clinic?

keyIdeas.idea: Writing each token fetches every weight, so the memory road sets its speed: 14 ms a token, at most about 71 a second, on both cards
More sums a second only speeds up reading the prompt, which is math-limited; writing does about one sum per byte and the adders wait
Time it on their own notes before switching, and compare memory speed per dollar and cost per million tokens

recall.model: Writing each token fetches every weight once: 14 billion bytes ÷ 1,000 GB/s = 14 ms, at most about 71 tokens a second on either card, because the memory road sets the speed, not the adders. Writing for one person does about one sum per byte, so it is memory-bound and the adders sit idle. Twice the TFLOPS only shortens reading the prompt, which is math-limited and already quick. So the answers won't come twice as fast. I'd time the offered card on their own notes before switching, and compare the cards by memory speed per dollar and cost per million tokens.

recall.prompt: On the A100, writing a token for one person does about 1 sum for each byte it fetches, and the card could do about 153. What sets the writing speed?
recall.why: 1 sum per byte is far below the card's ratio of 153, so the adders wait on the memory road: 16.06 billion bytes ÷ 2,039 GB/s = 7.9 ms a token, at most 127 a second. The sums a second only limit jobs above the ratio, like reading a 2,000-token question.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: why is generating text usually memory-bound on a GPU, and why does serving many users at once help?

keyIdeas.idea: Each new token needs every weight fetched from memory once
About one sum per byte: the arithmetic intensity is far below the card's ops:byte ratio, so the adders wait
One fetch of the weights serves every answer in the same step, so many users share it

recall.model: Each new token needs every weight fetched from the card's memory once: about 16 GB per token for an 8-billion-weight model in 16 bits. It does only about one sum per byte with them, so its arithmetic intensity is far below the card's ops:byte ratio (about 153 on an A100), and the adders sit idle while the memory road delivers. Serving many users helps because one fetch of the weights serves every answer in the same step: they share it, in a batch, so each step writes many tokens for nearly the price of one.

recall.prompt: The L40S costs $1.54 an hour and writes about 43 tokens a second for one person. About what does a million tokens cost?
recall.why: 43 × 3,600 = 154,800 tokens an hour, and $1.54 ÷ 154,800 × 1,000,000 = $9.95. The A100 at $2.79 an hour writes about 100 a second, 360,000 an hour, so $7.75: the cheaper card costs more per token.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Back on the A100 since 00:00 on Friday 2 October, checklists in 6 s again, and every card change now timed on our own answers first. On Monday 11 January 2027 the day shift's furnace crew started using the assistant too, and at the 06:00 shift change up to 8 of us ask at once. Venkatesh says each of the 8 gets an eighth of the road, about 12 tokens a second, so we need 8 cards: $16,294 a month. The dashboard says a step with 8 answers in it takes 12 ms.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is Venkatesh right that 8 people asking at once need 8 cards? What does each person get, and what does a million tokens cost?

keyIdeas.idea: One fetch of the weights serves every answer in the step, so the 8 share it rather than splitting the road
Each still gets about 83 tokens a second, 667 a second in all
One card is enough, and the cost per million falls to about $1.16

coldCase.model: No. Writing fetches every weight once per step, and that one fetch is shared by every answer in the step: the dashboard's 12 ms for 8 answers, against 10.25 ms for one. So each of the 8 still gets about 83 a second (1,000 ÷ 12), 667 a second in all, on one card. A million tokens then costs $2.79 ÷ (667 × 3,600, about 2.4 million an hour) × 1,000,000 = $1.16 per million, against $7.75 for one person at a time. Eight cards at $16,294 a month would make nobody faster.
